screens.title: Your First Godot Scene
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of Godot's fundamental structure: nodes as atomic units, scenes as reusable collections of nodes, and the scene tree that organizes them. You'll learn why nodes exist, how scenes let you compose and reuse groups of nodes across levels, and how parent-child relationships determine position, rotation, and behavior inheritance. We'll also attach a simple GDScript and observe the _ready callback and the print function in action when you run a scene. These ideas are essential because Godot's workflow depends on composing reusable scenes and moving behavior into scripts attached to nodes. A concrete example you will work with is creating a GameWorld root node, instancing a Player scene inside it, and attaching a script that prints a startup message to the Output panel. Common mistakes include wrong node paths and forgetting to save scenes or scripts; we'll highlight how to avoid those traps. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to instantiate scenes, navigate the scene tree reliably, and run a scene to confirm your scripted behavior. Consider how modular scenes could simplify updating a player object used across many levels.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice on Godot's composition model and basic scripting. First, you will deepen your understanding of Nodes as the atomic building blocks in Godot and be able to name examples like Sprite2D, Camera2D, and CharacterBody2D and describe their roles. Second, you will understand Scenes as reusable collections saved as. tscn files and explain why instancing scenes saves work across levels. Third, you will learn the Scene Tree: how parent and child relationships cause a child to inherit position, rotation, and scale and why that matters for grouping visual parts. Fourth, you will instantiate an existing scene into another scene to compose a level without copying nodes by hand. Each objective includes practice that reinforces the skill: inspecting node types in the Scene dock, instancing a Player scene into a GameWorld, and verifying transform inheritance by moving a parent. As you practice, watch for a common misconception: nodes are not loose objects; their behavior and transform depend on where they sit in the tree. These objectives prepare you to attach scripts and run scenes confidently.

screens.title: Nodes: Godot's Fundamental Building Blocks
screens.narratorSegment: A node is the most basic unit in Godot — a small object with a specific purpose such as rendering, physics, audio, or transform information. Define a node as a component that provides one responsibility: a Sprite2D draws an image, Camera2D defines the viewport, AudioStreamPlayer emits sound, and CharacterBody2D handles character physics. This single-responsibility design makes nodes composable: you assemble multiple nodes into a meaningful scene. A concrete example is a Player scene with a CharacterBody2D root to handle movement, a Sprite2D child for visuals, and a CollisionShape2D to define its hitbox. Beginners often misunderstand nodes as independent entities; instead, nodes gain context from the scene and their parent. That means choosing the right node type matters: using Node2D when you just need a transform, or CharacterBody2D when you need built-in physics integration. When you build, think of nodes as Lego pieces: pick pieces that fit the role you need and connect them into scenes. Your takeaway: knowing node types and responsibilities reduces work and prevents adding unnecessary logic to nodes that are not designed for it. Nodes: Godot's Fundamental Building Blocks means nodes are focused components; choose types by responsibility and combine them to form game objects.. In practical terms, what a node is, common node roles, and why nodes matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Node Definition
keyIdea.text: Nodes are focused components; choose types by responsibility and combine them to form game objects.

content.html:
Core Concept
Nodes: focused responsibilities
Each node provides a single role. Combine nodes to create richer behavior and structure.
Sprite2D
Renders a 2D texture; use for visuals.
Camera2D
Defines what part of the world the player sees.
CharacterBody2D
Built-in movement and collision behaviors for player characters.
Example: Player Scene
Root: CharacterBody2D • Child: Sprite2D • Child: CollisionShape2D
Analogy
Consider nodes as electronic components: a speaker plays sound, a light emits light. Wiring them together creates a device. Choose the right component to make the device work well.
Key Takeaway

Pick node types by responsibility and compose scenes from specialized nodes for predictable behavior.

screens.title: Common Node Types and When to Use Them
screens.narratorSegment: Godot provides many specialized node types. Understanding these categories helps you pick the right node and avoid adding unnecessary logic. Visual nodes like Sprite2D or MeshInstance3D handle drawing; use Sprite2D for 2D images. Transform nodes such as Node2D or Node3D provide position, rotation, and scale without additional behavior — use them when you need grouping or a pivot. Physics nodes like CharacterBody2D or RigidBody3D include built-in physics handling for movement and collision; pick CharacterBody2D when you control a player-like actor. Audio nodes such as AudioStreamPlayer play sounds and are best when you want spatial or timed audio. A concrete example: give a character a CharacterBody2D root to handle physics, add a Sprite2D for visuals, and an AudioStreamPlayer for footsteps. A common misconception is to attach movement code to a Sprite2D; instead keep movement in the physics node and visuals in Sprite2D. This separation keeps scenes modular and easier to reuse. Your practical rule: put behavior where the engine expects it and visuals where rendering is handled. Comparison
Node categories
Visual — Sprite2D
Draws images. Keep rendering separate from logic.
Transform — Node2D

screens.title: Scenes: Reusable Collections of Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: A scene in Godot is a saved collection of nodes arranged hierarchically and stored as a. tscn file. Scenes let you bundle a root node and its children into a single reusable component. For instance, a Player scene may include movement code, visuals, and collision shapes; once saved, you can instance the Player scene into many levels without rebuilding its internal nodes. This is powerful during development: change the original Player scene and every instance in other levels reflects that update automatically. That reduces duplication and keeps behaviors consistent across your project. A common beginner error is copying nodes manually into another scene rather than instancing the. tscn file; this creates maintenance burden because fixes won't propagate. Think of scenes as prefabricated components: they encapsulate structure, assets, and scripts so you can compose levels quickly. Your practical habit should be to design small, focused scenes that represent single game objects or subsystems and instance them where needed. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scene Definition
keyIdea.text: Scenes encapsulate nodes and their scripts into reusable .tscn files to promote modularity and easier updates.

content.html:
Definition
Scenes: saved node hierarchies

Save a group of nodes as a scene file so it can be instanced elsewhere. Scenes keep related nodes, resources, and scripts together.

Analogy
Treat a scene like a prefab: design once, reuse many times. Fix it once at the source and all instances update.
Example Scene File
# Player.tscn (simplified)
[ext_resource path="res://Player.gd" type="Script" id=1]
[node name="Player" type="CharacterBody2D"]
script = ExtResource( 1 )
[node name="Sprite2D" type="Sprite2D" parent="."]
texture = null
[node name="CollisionShape2D" type="CollisionShape2D" parent="."]
shape = null
Key Takeaway

Use scenes to package node groups; prefer instancing over manual copying to keep projects maintainable.

screens.title: Instancing a Scene into Another Scene
screens.narratorSegment: Instancing lets you add a saved scene into another scene quickly and reliably. The process is straightforward in the editor: create or open a parent scene such as GameWorld with a Node2D root. Then use the Instance Child Scene action in the Scene dock to select the Player. tscn file; the editor places an instance of Player as a child of GameWorld. Repeat for other reusable scenes like Enemy. tscn. This preserves every internal node defined inside Player, including scripts and resources. An example workflow: your Player has a movement script and sprite; when instanced, those behaviors are available immediately in the parent scene and will reflect future changes made to Player. tscn. A common misconception is that an instance is a disconnected copy — it is not. The instance links to the original. tscn so updates propagate. If you need an overridden property for a particular level, use scene inheritance or local overrides; otherwise rely on the shared source to reduce duplication. Instancing keeps levels consistent and speeds development. Instancing a Scene into Another Scene means use 'instance child scene' to add a linked copy of a .tscn file into another scene and preserve encapsulation and updates.. In practical terms, step-by-step composition: add player.tscn to gameworld. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow
Instancing steps
1
Create/Open parent scene
Example: GameWorld with Node2D root already open.
2
Instance Child Scene
Use the chain-link icon in the Scene dock and select Player.tscn from the file system.
3
Confirm hierarchy
An instance node appears as a child; open it to inspect internal nodes.

screens.title: Scene Tree and Parent-Child Transform Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: The Scene Tree is the hierarchical structure that organizes nodes inside a scene. Each entry is a node with zero or more children; a child's transform is defined relative to its parent. Practically, this means a child at position (10,10) under a parent at (100,50) will appear at world position (110,60). Use this property to group related parts — for example, attach a Gun node as a child of Player so it moves and rotates with the player automatically. A common misunderstanding is thinking child nodes have independent absolute positions; in fact their coordinates are local to the parent. This behavior is useful for animation and pivoting: rotating a parent rotates all its children around the parent's pivot. When designing your scene tree, organize nodes by logical grouping and expected shared transform. It simplifies movement, camera following, and complex composed behaviors. Test transform inheritance by moving a parent in the editor to observe child movement immediately. Scene Tree and Parent-Child Transform Inheritance means a child's transform adds to the parent's transform; use grouping to manage coordinated motion and rotation.. In practical terms, how a child's position is defined relative to its parent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transform Inheritance
keyIdea.text: A child's transform adds to the parent's transform; use grouping to manage coordinated motion and rotation.

content.html:
Process Flow
Scene Tree: parent → child relationships
Child transforms are relative to their parent. Use this to group parts that should move together and to create consistent pivots for rotation.
Concrete calculation
Parent position: (100, 50) Child local position: (10, 10) Child world position = (100 + 10, 50 + 10) = (110, 60)
Scenario
Attach a Gun node to Player so it follows movement and rotation.
Key Takeaway

Organize nodes by shared transform to simplify motion, animation, and camera composition.

screens.title: Practical Editor Steps: Create GameWorld and Instance Players
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete editor workflow to assemble a level using instanced scenes. First, create a new 2D scene and add a Node2D root; rename it to GameWorld and save it as GameWorld. tscn. Second, ensure you have Player. tscn and Enemy. tscn in your project files. Third, in the Scene dock use Instance Child Scene to add Player. tscn — confirm it appears as a child of GameWorld. Fourth, repeat for Enemy. tscn so GameWorld contains both instanced children. Fifth, inspect each instance and verify internal nodes like Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D are present. This sequence avoids re-creating nodes and preserves the link to each source scene so you can update the player or enemy once and have changes propagate. A common mistake is forgetting to save these scenes after changes; always save the. tscn files and script files before running the scene. Finally, run the current scene to validate everything loads as expected and to check console messages from attached scripts. screens.title: Accessing Child Nodes: get_node, $ shorthand, and @onready
screens.narratorSegment: Accessing child nodes from a script is a frequent task and there are several idiomatic ways to do it. The direct method is get_node with a path string like get_node("Sprite2D"), which works but is a runtime lookup. The shorthand $Sprite2D is faster to type and more common in examples. Use @onready var my_sprite = $Sprite2D to cache the reference once the node is available; this ensures the variable is prepared after the node enters the scene tree. If a child is nested, use a path like $Visuals/Sprite2D to reach it. A common mistake is using get_node with an incorrect relative path from the script's owner node; paths are relative to the node that owns the script. Concrete example: in Main. gd use @onready to capture $Sprite2D and then adjust its position inside _ready. This pattern reduces repeated lookups and makes your code clearer and more robust against runtime errors. keyIdea.title: Node Access Patterns
keyIdea.text: Prefer the $ shorthand and @onready caching for readable, reliable access to child nodes from scripts.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Accessing child nodes
Use the $ shorthand for direct child lookups and @onready to cache references safely.
# Example snippet
extends Node2D
@onready var my_sprite = $Sprite2D

func _ready():
  if my_sprite:
    print("Sprite2D found! Its name is: ", my_sprite.name)
    my_sprite.position.x += 50
  else:
    print("Sprite2D not found as a child of Main.")
Best practices
  • Cache references with @onready to avoid repeated lookups.
  • Use relative paths like $Visuals/Sprite2D for nested children.
  • Confirm the node exists before accessing its properties to avoid runtime errors.
Key Takeaway

Node paths are relative to the script owner. Use $ and @onready to write clearer, safer code.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners encounter a few recurring mistakes when working with scenes and scripts. First, incorrect node paths cause runtime errors: if you ask for a child that isn't where you expect, get_node returns an error and your script may fail. The fix is to verify the path relative to the script owner, or use @onready caching with the $ shorthand. Second, forgetting to save scenes or scripts before running causes surprises because the editor runs older versions of your work; adopt a habit of saving before testing. Third, placing behavior on the wrong node — for example, putting movement code on a Sprite2D instead of on a physics node — creates harder-to-maintain scenes. A concrete remediation is to place behavior in CharacterBody2D for physics-based movement and keep Sprite2D for visuals. A useful practice is to run Play Current often, watch the Output panel for print messages, and inspect the instanced scene to confirm internal node names. These small checks prevent long debugging sessions and keep development moving smoothly. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important concepts from this chapter. First, a Node is a focused component that provides a single responsibility such as rendering, physics, or audio. Second, a Scene is a saved collection of nodes in a. tscn file that you can instance elsewhere, allowing reuse and centralized updates. Third, the Scene Tree organizes nodes hierarchically so children inherit transform from their parent; this is central to grouping and animation. These three ideas are the backbone of building in Godot: select appropriate node types, package them into scenes, and arrange them in a scene tree to produce composed behavior. Keep these concepts visible as you design: they shape how you structure scenes, attach scripts, and iterate quickly with Play Current. A quick practice reminder: when you see unexpected behavior, check node types, instance links, and node paths first.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a clear mental model of Godot's fundamental structure: nodes as atomic units, scenes as reusable collections of nodes, and the scene tree that organizes them. You'll learn why nodes exist, how scenes let you compose and reuse groups of nodes across levels, and how parent-child relationships determine position, rotation, and behavior inheritance. We'll also attach a simple GDScript and observe the _ready callback and the print function in action when you run a scene. These ideas are essential because Godot's workflow depends on composing reusable scenes and moving behavior into scripts attached to nodes. A concrete example you will work with is creating a GameWorld root node, instancing a Player scene inside it, and attaching a script that prints a startup message to the Output panel. Common mistakes include wrong node paths and forgetting to save scenes or scripts; we'll highlight how to avoid those traps. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to instantiate scenes, navigate the scene tree reliably, and run a scene to confirm your scripted behavior. Consider how modular scenes could simplify updating a player object used across many levels.

These objectives focus your practice on Godot's composition model and basic scripting. First, you will deepen your understanding of Nodes as the atomic building blocks in Godot and be able to name examples like Sprite2D, Camera2D, and CharacterBody2D and describe their roles. Second, you will understand Scenes as reusable collections saved as. tscn files and explain why instancing scenes saves work across levels. Third, you will learn the Scene Tree: how parent and child relationships cause a child to inherit position, rotation, and scale and why that matters for grouping visual parts. Fourth, you will instantiate an existing scene into another scene to compose a level without copying nodes by hand. Each objective includes practice that reinforces the skill: inspecting node types in the Scene dock, instancing a Player scene into a GameWorld, and verifying transform inheritance by moving a parent. As you practice, watch for a common misconception: nodes are not loose objects; their behavior and transform depend on where they sit in the tree. These objectives prepare you to attach scripts and run scenes confidently.

These additional objectives prepare you to attach scripts, run scenes, and avoid common mistakes. You will attach a GDScript to a node, write a simple _ready callback, and use the print function to confirm behavior in the Output panel. You will run a single open scene with Play Current and understand the difference when you set a main scene and run the whole project. You will also learn practical checks for common pitfalls: verifying node paths using the dollar shorthand, saving scenes and scripts before running, and inspecting the Output panel for runtime messages. Finally, you'll practice a small hands-on activity that combines these skills: add a Camera2D, attach a script to the root, move a sprite programmatically, and observe console messages. Each skill is directly useful: scripts bring nodes to life, running the scene confirms behavior, and careful path usage prevents runtime errors.

A node is the most basic unit in Godot — a small object with a specific purpose such as rendering, physics, audio, or transform information. Define a node as a component that provides one responsibility: a Sprite2D draws an image, Camera2D defines the viewport, AudioStreamPlayer emits sound, and CharacterBody2D handles character physics. This single-responsibility design makes nodes composable: you assemble multiple nodes into a meaningful scene. A concrete example is a Player scene with a CharacterBody2D root to handle movement, a Sprite2D child for visuals, and a CollisionShape2D to define its hitbox. Beginners often misunderstand nodes as independent entities; instead, nodes gain context from the scene and their parent. That means choosing the right node type matters: using Node2D when you just need a transform, or CharacterBody2D when you need built-in physics integration. When you build, think of nodes as Lego pieces: pick pieces that fit the role you need and connect them into scenes. Your takeaway: knowing node types and responsibilities reduces work and prevents adding unnecessary logic to nodes that are not designed for it. Nodes: Godot's Fundamental Building Blocks means nodes are focused components; choose types by responsibility and combine them to form game objects.. In practical terms, what a node is, common node roles, and why nodes matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Godot provides many specialized node types. Understanding these categories helps you pick the right node and avoid adding unnecessary logic. Visual nodes like Sprite2D or MeshInstance3D handle drawing; use Sprite2D for 2D images. Transform nodes such as Node2D or Node3D provide position, rotation, and scale without additional behavior — use them when you need grouping or a pivot. Physics nodes like CharacterBody2D or RigidBody3D include built-in physics handling for movement and collision; pick CharacterBody2D when you control a player-like actor. Audio nodes such as AudioStreamPlayer play sounds and are best when you want spatial or timed audio. A concrete example: give a character a CharacterBody2D root to handle physics, add a Sprite2D for visuals, and an AudioStreamPlayer for footsteps. A common misconception is to attach movement code to a Sprite2D; instead keep movement in the physics node and visuals in Sprite2D. This separation keeps scenes modular and easier to reuse. Your practical rule: put behavior where the engine expects it and visuals where rendering is handled. Common Node Types and When to Use Them means select node types by their built-in responsibilities to simplify your code and reuse scenes.. In practical terms, visual, transform, physics, and audio nodes explained with examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A scene in Godot is a saved collection of nodes arranged hierarchically and stored as a. tscn file. Scenes let you bundle a root node and its children into a single reusable component. For instance, a Player scene may include movement code, visuals, and collision shapes; once saved, you can instance the Player scene into many levels without rebuilding its internal nodes. This is powerful during development: change the original Player scene and every instance in other levels reflects that update automatically. That reduces duplication and keeps behaviors consistent across your project. A common beginner error is copying nodes manually into another scene rather than instancing the. tscn file; this creates maintenance burden because fixes won't propagate. Think of scenes as prefabricated components: they encapsulate structure, assets, and scripts so you can compose levels quickly. Your practical habit should be to design small, focused scenes that represent single game objects or subsystems and instance them where needed. Instancing lets you add a saved scene into another scene quickly and reliably. The process is straightforward in the editor: create or open a parent scene such as GameWorld with a Node2D root. Then use the Instance Child Scene action in the Scene dock to select the Player. tscn file; the editor places an instance of Player as a child of GameWorld. Repeat for other reusable scenes like Enemy. tscn. This preserves every internal node defined inside Player, including scripts and resources. An example workflow: your Player has a movement script and sprite; when instanced, those behaviors are available immediately in the parent scene and will reflect future changes made to Player. tscn. A common misconception is that an instance is a disconnected copy — it is not. The instance links to the original. tscn so updates propagate. If you need an overridden property for a particular level, use scene inheritance or local overrides; otherwise rely on the shared source to reduce duplication. Instancing keeps levels consistent and speeds development. The Scene Tree is the hierarchical structure that organizes nodes inside a scene. Each entry is a node with zero or more children; a child's transform is defined relative to its parent. Practically, this means a child at position (10,10) under a parent at (100,50) will appear at world position (110,60). Use this property to group related parts — for example, attach a Gun node as a child of Player so it moves and rotates with the player automatically. A common misunderstanding is thinking child nodes have independent absolute positions; in fact their coordinates are local to the parent. This behavior is useful for animation and pivoting: rotating a parent rotates all its children around the parent's pivot. When designing your scene tree, organize nodes by logical grouping and expected shared transform. It simplifies movement, camera following, and complex composed behaviors. Test transform inheritance by moving a parent in the editor to observe child movement immediately. Running your work is the fast way to verify behavior. In Godot, Play Current Scene runs the scene you currently have open, which is ideal for testing a specific part like GameWorld. tscn. Play Project launches the project's main scene defined in Project Settings; use it to test the full game flow. A common beginner confusion is expecting Play Project to always run the open scene — it runs the main scene instead. If you want the current scene to launch with Play Project, set it as the main scene when prompted. Use Play Current when iterating quickly on a single scene and Play Project when you want to see startup sequences and the full initial flow. After running, check the Output panel for messages from print calls in _ready; these messages are the simplest evidence your script ran. Accessing child nodes from a script is a frequent task and there are several idiomatic ways to do it. The direct method is get_node with a path string like get_node("Sprite2D"), which works but is a runtime lookup. The shorthand $Sprite2D is faster to type and more common in examples. Use @onready var my_sprite = $Sprite2D to cache the reference once the node is available; this ensures the variable is prepared after the node enters the scene tree. If a child is nested, use a path like $Visuals/Sprite2D to reach it. A common mistake is using get_node with an incorrect relative path from the script's owner node; paths are relative to the node that owns the script. Concrete example: in Main. gd use @onready to capture $Sprite2D and then adjust its position inside _ready. This pattern reduces repeated lookups and makes your code clearer and more robust against runtime errors. Beginners encounter a few recurring mistakes when working with scenes and scripts. First, incorrect node paths cause runtime errors: if you ask for a child that isn't where you expect, get_node returns an error and your script may fail. The fix is to verify the path relative to the script owner, or use @onready caching with the $ shorthand. Second, forgetting to save scenes or scripts before running causes surprises because the editor runs older versions of your work; adopt a habit of saving before testing. Third, placing behavior on the wrong node — for example, putting movement code on a Sprite2D instead of on a physics node — creates harder-to-maintain scenes. A concrete remediation is to place behavior in CharacterBody2D for physics-based movement and keep Sprite2D for visuals. A useful practice is to run Play Current often, watch the Output panel for print messages, and inspect the instanced scene to confirm internal node names. These small checks prevent long debugging sessions and keep development moving smoothly. Let's summarize the most important concepts from this chapter. First, a Node is a focused component that provides a single responsibility such as rendering, physics, or audio. Second, a Scene is a saved collection of nodes in a. tscn file that you can instance elsewhere, allowing reuse and centralized updates. Third, the Scene Tree organizes nodes hierarchically so children inherit transform from their parent; this is central to grouping and animation. These three ideas are the backbone of building in Godot: select appropriate node types, package them into scenes, and arrange them in a scene tree to produce composed behavior. Keep these concepts visible as you design: they shape how you structure scenes, attach scripts, and iterate quickly with Play Current. A quick practice reminder: when you see unexpected behavior, check node types, instance links, and node paths first.

Before you close this lesson, keep a short developer checklist in mind. First, always choose node types that match responsibility — rendering nodes for visuals, physics nodes for movement. Second, prefer instancing scenes rather than copying node trees so updates propagate across your project. Third, use the $ shorthand and @onready caching to access child nodes safely and reduce runtime lookups. Fourth, save your scenes and scripts before running to ensure the latest code executes. These checkpoints help you avoid the most common problems beginners face and make it easier to scale your project. As you practice, ask yourself: did I pick the right node type, did I instance instead of copy, and did I save before running? These three quick checks will save you debugging time.
